summary: A status report on a proposed Data Reconfiguration Service, a network service to translate data from the form one computer produces into the form another expects. It covers the purpose, motivation and design so far. RFC 166 gives the implementation specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people speak different languages, so a helper in the middle translates. This report describes the plan for a computer translator for data.

questions: what is the data reconfiguration service
why was a data translation service proposed
how were data formats converted on the early arpanet
subtitle: A 1971 proposal for a network service that reshapes data streams using named, stored rules called forms.

tldr.problem: Programs and consoles on the network expect different data formats, and changing every program to follow one standard is costly.
tldr.mechanism: A Data Reconfiguration Service stores named forms, written in a small rule notation, and applies a form to a data stream passing between a user process and a server process.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes a proposed experiment and asks for comments. Four sites planned to implement it.

today: RFC 138 is a 1971 status report that asked for comments on an experiment, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a plan, not a finished standard.

sections.title: The Idea and Its Motivation
sections.content:
Application programs need specific data formats, and those formats differ from program to program. The authors take the position that the network should adapt to each program, rather than changing each program to follow a standard. They want comments on whether this is an appropriate network experiment and on reformatting needs it could not easily meet.

A programmer defines forms that describe a reconfiguration, and the service stores them by name. Later a user, perhaps a non-programmer, calls a form by name to transform a data stream. The notation is meant to be more expressive than a trivial one but short of a general purpose programming language.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of making every toy fit the same box, a helper reshapes each toy so it fits whichever box it is going into.

sections.title: Connections and Commands
sections.content:
The service has three conceptual connections. The control connection (CC) links the originating user and the service, and forms are defined over it. The user connection (UC) runs between the user process and the service, and the server connection (SC) runs between the service and the serving process. Only a minimum is required of the UC and SC.

A user reaches the service with the initial connection protocol of RFC 80, calling a socket on which it always listens. Control messages follow the TELNET formats. The user supplies a six-character user ID so form names stay unique, and has commands such as DEFFORM, ENDFORM, PURGE, LISTNAMES, LISTFORM, DUPLEXCONNECT and SIMPLEXCONNECT. A connection can be made as an already connected dummy control connection, by standard ICP (duplex only), or directly with STR and RTS.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one line for giving instructions to the translator, one line from you to it, and one line from it to the program you want to talk to.

sections.title: The Form Machine
sections.content:
The Form Machine reads an input stream, reformats it as a form directs, and emits an output stream. A form is an ordered set of rules. Each rule has an optional integer label from 0 to 9999, an input part to match, and an output part after a colon, and it ends with a semicolon. If the input part fails, another rule is tried. If it succeeds, data may be emitted and both stream pointers advance.

Rules are built from terms. A descriptor has a replication expression, a data type, a value expression and a length expression. The data types are B (bit string, 1 bit units), O (3 bits), X (4 bits), E (EBCDIC character, 8 bits) and A (Network ASCII character, 8 bits). The arbitrary-length symbol means a field of any length, ended by the next term, and is legal only in the input stream. Control options S, F and U transfer to a rule on success, failure or unconditionally, and R ends the form with a return code. Limits include identifiers of at most 4 characters, at most 256 identifiers and character strings of at most 256 characters. Arithmetic is evaluated left to right with no precedence.
sections.plainLanguage: A form is a list of little matching rules, like a recipe that says: find this piece, then write it out in this other way.

sections.title: Examples, Uses and Plans
sections.content:
The examples show field insertion (line numbering for a 121-character line printer), deletion, variable-length records, prefixing a length to a string, transposition of fields, and packing and unpacking repeated EBCDIC characters. Proposed uses from the sites include packing and unpacking text files, character conversions, reformatting within a file transfer service, and describing message formats of remote job services.

Four sites planned to implement it on an experimental basis: MIT, UCLA, UCSB and RAND. The University of Illinois and Mitre planned to experiment with it. An appendix records open questions from the working group, including how to define the arbitrary-length symbol and whether the input pointer should advance after each term or after a whole rule.
sections.plainLanguage: Many sites wanted the translator for jobs like swapping letter codes or reordering columns, and several planned to build one to try it.
